_note: PTB-XL v1.0.3 (CC BY 4.0). Waveforms real; teaching text being drafted and reviewed.

rois.R: Rate about 60, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, consistent shape. Upright P waves in the inferior leads.
rois.I: PR interval normal, QRS narrow, QT proportionate to the rate.
rois.S: Baseline ST segments throughout. Upright T waves where expected. This is your reference for what normal looks like.

rois.R: Rate about 65, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, consistent.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow, QT normal.
rois.S: No ST shift; normal T waves.

records.label: Normal sinus

rois.R: Rate about 70, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS. Note the brief baseline step in V2 early on — a lead artefact, not a cardiac event; worth pointing out to a learner.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow, QT normal.
rois.S: No ST shift; normal T waves.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm (with a minor lead artefact in V2)

rois.R: Rate about 60, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, consistent.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow, QT normal.
rois.S: No ST shift; normal T waves.

rois.R: Rate about 85, regular, sinus. Tall QRS in the chest leads — common in a fit young person, not itself abnormal.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow, QT normal.
rois.S: No ST shift; normal T waves.

records.label: First degree AV block

rois.R: Rate about 68, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, each P followed by a QRS. Consistent P shape.
rois.I: The PR interval is long — the gap from P to QRS is stretched beyond one large square. QRS narrow. This prolonged PR is the whole finding.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift across the territories.

findings: Prolonged PR interval (first degree AV block)

rois.R: Rate about 75, regular, sinus.
rois.O: P before each QRS. Note lead II here is drifting with baseline wander — read the rhythm off a cleaner lead like V2 or aVL.
rois.I: Prolonged PR interval. QRS narrow.
rois.S: No clear ST change; baseline wander in the limb leads makes the ST hard to trust.

rois.R: Rate about 98, regular, sinus. On the quicker side of normal.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: Prolonged PR interval. QRS narrow.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift across the territories.

rois.R: Irregularly irregular — this one is in AF, so no regular rhythm. Rate around 75.
rois.O: No organised P waves (AF). Don't stop there — look at the QRS.
rois.I: The QRS is broad, over three small squares. Broad QRS is the bundle branch block finding.
rois.S: In left bundle branch block the ST and T are expected to point opposite to the main QRS — assess with that in mind, don't read it like a normal ST.

rois.R: Rate about 75, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: Broad QRS. Note the characteristic notched/slurred R wave in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6).
rois.S: ST and T discordant to the QRS, as expected in left bundle branch block — don't over-read it.

rois.R: Rate about 90, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: Broad QRS with the left bundle branch block morphology through the lateral and chest leads.
rois.S: ST and T discordant to the QRS, expected in left bundle branch block.

records.label: Right bundle branch block

rois.R: Rate about 70, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: Broad QRS. Look at V1 for the right bundle branch block signature — the second R wave (an RSR', 'rabbit ears') — and the wide S wave in the lateral leads.
rois.S: Assess the T waves in the context of the wide QRS.

findings: Right bundle branch block (RSR' in V1)

rois.R: Irregularly irregular — in AF. Rate around 55. Baseline wander in the limb leads.
rois.O: No organised P waves (AF).
rois.I: Broad QRS with right bundle branch block morphology (RSR' in V1).
rois.S: Assess the T waves with the wide QRS in mind.

rois.R: Rate about 90, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: Broad QRS, RSR' in V1 — a clean right bundle branch block example.
rois.S: T waves assessed with the wide QRS in mind.

records.label: Incomplete RBBB

rois.R: Rate about 70, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, upright in II.
rois.I: QRS not broad. Look at V1 and V2: there is a small second upward bump at the end of the QRS (an rSR' shape). That extra bump with a QRS that is not broad is the incomplete right bundle branch block pattern.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

findings: Incomplete right bundle branch block (rSR' in V1–V2, QRS not broad)

records.label: Incomplete RBBB

rois.R: Rate about 70, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: QRS not broad. V1 shows an rSR' shape, with a clear second R wave, and there is a small slurred S wave in I and V6. A complete right bundle branch block has the same shape with a broad QRS; here the width stays under three small squares.
rois.S: T wave inverted in V1, which is common with this pattern. No convincing ST shift elsewhere.

findings: Incomplete right bundle branch block (rSR' in V1)

rois.R: Rate about 72, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: QRS narrow. Now check the axis: I and aVL are mainly positive, while II, III and aVF are mainly negative (small r, deep S). That is left axis deviation, and with a narrow QRS this is the left anterior fascicular block pattern.
rois.S: No ST shift. T waves follow the QRS as expected.

rois.R: Rate about 63, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: QRS narrow. Axis: I is positive, but II, III and aVF are mainly negative. That is left axis deviation, the key finding in left anterior fascicular block. Note the small QRS complexes in V1–V3.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift. Some baseline noise in the limb leads.

rois.R: Rate about 48, regular. Sinus bradycardia.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, upright in II.
rois.I: PR normal. The QRS is at the upper end of normal width without the shape of either bundle branch block. The dataset labels this a non-specific intraventricular conduction delay. It is subtle, and you may well read it as near-normal. Tall R waves in V4–V5.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

rois.R: Underlying rate about 80. Not regular: several beats arrive early.
rois.O: Most beats have a P wave before them. The early beats (around 1.9 s and 7.6 s, and a different-looking one near 9.1 s) have no P wave before them and a broad, bizarre QRS. These are ventricular ectopics, and they are not all the same shape.
rois.I: On the normal beats: PR normal. The dataset labels this an intraventricular conduction delay, a subtle widening of the QRS without a bundle branch block shape, but the ectopics are the more obvious finding here.
rois.S: Assess the ST and T on the normal beats only. The ectopic beats have their own abnormal ST/T, which is expected. Noisy baseline in II, III and aVF.

records.label: Left ventricular hypertrophy

rois.R: Rate about 86, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: QRS narrow. Look at the size: a very deep S wave in V1–V2 and very tall R waves in V5–V6. S in V1 plus R in V5 comes to roughly 49 small squares, well above the usual voltage threshold of 35. That is the left ventricular hypertrophy voltage pattern.
rois.S: Subtle ST depression with flattened T waves in the lateral leads. This is often seen alongside the voltage changes and is sometimes called a strain pattern.

findings: Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage (deep S V1–V2, tall R V5–V6)

rois.R: Not regular. The underlying sinus rhythm is interrupted by frequent early beats. Rate about 70 overall.
rois.O: The normal beats have a P wave before them. The early beats (for example around 2.0 s, 3.7 s, 7.8 s and 9.6 s) are broad and bizarre with no P wave before them. These are ventricular ectopics.
rois.I: Measure on the normal beats: QRS narrow. Large QRS voltages, particularly the deep S in V1–V2 and tall R in aVL. That is the left ventricular hypertrophy finding.
rois.S: Judge the ST and T on the normal beats only. The ectopics have their own broad, opposite-pointing ST/T, which is expected and not a separate finding.

records.label: Left ventricular hypertrophy

rois.R: Rate about 65, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: QRS narrow. Tall R waves in V5–V6 with deep S waves in V2–V3. The dataset labels this left ventricular hypertrophy, but on this tracing the voltages are borderline rather than obvious, a reminder that the ECG is not a sensitive test for hypertrophy.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift. Low, flat T waves in III and aVL.

findings: Left ventricular hypertrophy (labelled by dataset; borderline voltages)

records.label: Right ventricular hypertrophy

rois.R: Rate about 91, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: QRS narrow. Look at the right-sided chest leads: V1 has an R wave as tall as its S wave, which is unusual because V1 is normally mostly negative. V2–V3 have very tall R waves.
rois.S: T wave inversion in V1–V3. With the tall right-sided R waves, this is the right ventricular hypertrophy pattern with right ventricular strain.

findings: Right ventricular hypertrophy (tall R in V1–V3)

rois.R: Rate about 66, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: The PR interval is short, under three small squares, and the start of the QRS is slightly slurred in some leads. That slur is the delta wave. Here it is subtle, a good reminder that pre-excitation does not always look dramatic.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

records.label: Wolff-Parkinson-White

rois.R: Rate about 79, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: Look for the P wave just before each QRS. It sits very close to the QRS because the PR is short.
rois.I: The PR is short and the QRS is broad, with a slow, slurred upstroke at its start (the delta wave), best seen in I, aVL and V5–V6. Short PR, delta wave and broad QRS together make the Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern. Note the deep negative complexes in III and aVF: in this pattern they can mimic old infarct Q waves.
rois.S: ST and T point opposite to the main QRS in many leads, secondary to the abnormal conduction. Don't read it as ischaemia.

findings: Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern (short PR, delta wave, broad QRS)

rois.R: Rate about 105, fairly regular. Sinus tachycardia.
rois.O: P waves are small and hard to separate from the end of the T waves at this rate. Low-amplitude limb leads and a noisy baseline make this a real-world reading challenge.
rois.I: QRS narrow. QT is long: in V2–V4 the T wave finishes well past the halfway point between one R wave and the next. At this rate the QT should be shorter than that, so check the QT on every ECG, not just slow ones.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift. Broad T waves.

rois.R: Rate about 91, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow. The QT is long: from QRS start to T end is about 10 small squares, and the T wave ends past the halfway point between R waves. A useful quick check is that the T wave should end before the halfway point between two R waves.
rois.S: No ST shift. Broad T waves, which go with the long QT.

rois.R: Rate about 75, gently irregular — the rhythm varies with breathing (sinus arrhythmia). Sinus origin.
rois.O: A P wave before each QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow.
rois.S: Anteroseptal territory: look at V1–V2 (septal) and V3–V4 (anterior). The chest-lead complexes are very tall here and the baseline moves, so assess the ST segment carefully against the baseline before calling elevation.

rois.R: Rate about 63, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before each QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow.
rois.S: ST elevation in V1–V3 — the septal and anterior leads. This is the anteroseptal territory.

rois.R: Rate about 75, but look carefully — this is bigeminy: every other beat is an early, different-looking complex. Don't let the ectopics distract you from the underlying ECG.
rois.O: Sinus P waves underlie the conducted (normal) beats.
rois.I: Assess the intervals on the conducted sinus beats, not the ectopic ones.
rois.S: On the conducted sinus beats, ST elevation in V1–V3 — the anteroseptal territory.

rois.R: Rate about 75, regular. Sinus rhythm.
rois.O: A P wave before each QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow. Note marked baseline wander in V6 — a real-world reading challenge.
rois.S: Inferior territory: assess II, III and aVF (the inferior leads) for ST elevation, and check I and aVL for reciprocal change. The inferior complexes are low-amplitude here, so read the ST against the baseline carefully.

rois.R: Rate about 78, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before each QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow.
rois.S: Inferior territory: assess II, III and aVF. Note III and aVF show prominent deep negative deflections here — consider whether these are established Q waves as well as any ST change. Check I and aVL for reciprocal change.

rois.R: Rate about 90, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before each QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow.
rois.S: ST elevation in the inferior leads — II, III and aVF. Check I and aVL for reciprocal change.

records.label: Inferolateral MI

rois.R: Rate about 70, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before each QRS.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow.
rois.S: Inferolateral territory: two areas to scan — inferior (II, III, aVF) and lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6). The inferior leads are quiet and the lateral leads noisy here, so assess the ST carefully in both.

findings: Inferolateral MI (territory: II, III, aVF, and I, aVL, V5–V6)

rois.R: Rate about 60, regular, sinus.
rois.O: A P wave before each QRS.
rois.I: Broad QRS — this record also carries a right bundle branch block, which widens the QRS and changes its shape. Read the ST/T with that in mind.
rois.S: This is a multi-finding ECG: an inferolateral pattern (II, III, aVF and the lateral leads) alongside anteroseptal changes and a right bundle branch block. A good example of not stopping at the first finding — assess every territory.

records.label: Atrial fibrillation

rois.R: Irregularly irregular — no two R-R gaps the same. Rate around 90.
rois.O: No consistent P waves; the baseline is fibrillatory rather than showing organised P waves. Absence of P waves is the finding.
rois.I: QRS narrow.
rois.S: Assess by territory once the rhythm is established.

findings: Atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular, no P waves)

records.label: Atrial fibrillation

rois.R: Irregularly irregular, but slow — around 50. AF doesn't have to be fast.
rois.O: No organised P waves.
rois.I: QRS narrow.
rois.S: Assess by territory.

findings: Atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular response

records.label: Atrial fibrillation

rois.R: Irregularly irregular and fast — around 130+. The chest leads are busy and high-amplitude.
rois.O: No organised P waves.
rois.I: QRS narrow.
rois.S: Hard to assess ST at this rate.

findings: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response

records.label: Atrial flutter

rois.R: Regular or near-regular, and fast. Look at the baseline between the QRS complexes.
rois.O: Sawtooth flutter waves — best seen in II, III, aVF and V1. That sawtooth is the signature. No normal P waves.
rois.I: QRS narrow.
rois.S: Assess after the rhythm.

findings: Atrial flutter (sawtooth flutter waves, inferior leads and V1)

rois.R: Fast, fairly regular.
rois.O: Sawtooth flutter waves — again clearest in the inferior leads and V1.
rois.I: QRS narrow.
rois.S: Assess after the rhythm.

records.label: Supraventricular tachycardia

rois.R: Fast and regular, about 165. Narrow-complex tachycardia.
rois.O: No clear P wave before each QRS. The dataset also codes possible flutter activity: at this rate, flutter waves at 2:1 can hide in the T waves, so scan II, III, aVF and V1 between complexes.
rois.I: QRS narrow, so the rhythm is coming from above the ventricles.
rois.S: Hard to assess ST at this rate. Note what you see, but expect it to be less reliable during a fast tachycardia.

findings: Supraventricular tachycardia (possible 2:1 flutter coded by the dataset)

records.label: Supraventricular tachycardia

rois.R: Fast and regular, about 170. Narrow-complex tachycardia. (Every R-R gap is near-identical, even though the auto-measure called it irregular.)
rois.O: No normal P waves. Look at III and aVF: the baseline keeps undulating at roughly twice the QRS rate. That suggests flutter waves with 2:1 conduction, and the dataset codes atrial flutter as well as SVT. A regular rate near 150–170 should always make you hunt for hidden flutter waves.
rois.I: QRS narrow.
rois.S: Hard to assess ST at this rate.

findings: Flutter waves suggested in III and aVF (likely 2:1)

rois.R: Rate about 105, regular. Sinus tachycardia, with one early beat near the start.
rois.O: A P wave before each normal QRS. The second complex is early, broad and differently shaped with no P wave before it: a single ventricular ectopic. Don't let it distract you.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow on the sinus beats.
rois.S: No ST shift on the sinus beats.

rois.R: Rate about 105, regular. Sinus tachycardia.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS. At faster rates the P wave sits close to the preceding T wave, so look carefully.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow, QT normal for the rate.
rois.S: No ST shift. Some baseline drift in V1.

rois.R: Rate about 41, regular. Sinus bradycardia.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, consistent shape, upright in II.
rois.I: PR normal and constant, QRS narrow. Every P is followed by a QRS, so there is no block. This is simply a slow sinus rhythm.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

rois.R: Rate about 43, slightly irregular. Sinus bradycardia, with some variation in the gaps (a touch of sinus arrhythmia).
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, consistent shape.
rois.I: PR normal and constant, QRS narrow. One P to one QRS throughout.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

rois.R: Rate about 62, gently irregular. The gaps between beats lengthen and shorten in a smooth, repeating way rather than at random.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, all the same shape. Same-shape P waves with a varying rate means the rhythm is still sinus.
rois.I: PR normal and constant, QRS narrow.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

rois.R: Rate about 61, gently irregular. The gaps shorten in the middle of the strip and lengthen at the end, a smooth change typical of breathing.
rois.O: A P wave before every QRS, same shape throughout, so the rhythm is sinus.
rois.I: PR normal and constant, QRS narrow.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

rois.R: Irregular, but in a repeating pattern: beats come in pairs. A normal beat, then an early beat, then a pause. Overall rate about 90.
rois.O: Every second beat is early. The early beats are narrow and look like the normal beats, so they come from above the ventricles (atrial ectopics), not from the ventricles. Pairs like this are called bigeminy.
rois.I: QRS narrow on both the normal and the early beats.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift. Baseline drift in V1 and V6.

rois.R: Irregular in a repeating pattern: a normal beat, then an early broad beat, then a pause. Overall rate about 65.
rois.O: The normal beats have a P wave before them. The early beats are broad and bizarre with no P wave: ventricular ectopics. For most of the strip every second beat is an ectopic, which is ventricular bigeminy. Note the short run of normal beats in the middle where the pattern breaks.
rois.I: Assess the PR and QRS on the normal beats: QRS narrow.
rois.S: Judge ST and T on the normal beats only. Baseline artefact in V2–V3.

rois.R: Irregular in a repeating pattern of threes: two normal beats, then an early beat, then a pause. Overall rate about 85.
rois.O: Every third beat is early. The early beats are narrow and the same shape as the normal ones, so they are supraventricular (atrial) ectopics. A repeating pattern every third beat is trigeminy.
rois.I: QRS narrow on all beats.
rois.S: No ST shift. Normal T waves.

records.label: Paced rhythm

rois.R: Rate about 70, regular once the pacemaker takes over.
rois.O: The first one or two beats are different from the rest. After that, each broad QRS is preceded by a small, sharp spike, best seen in II and V5. That spike is the pacemaker firing. Pacing spikes can be tiny on a digital recording, so look hard.
rois.I: QRS broad on the paced beats. This is expected because the pacing lead activates the ventricles directly, not through the normal conduction system.
rois.S: ST and T point opposite to the main QRS on the paced beats. This is expected with pacing; don't read it as ischaemia.

findings: Paced rhythm (pacing spikes before a broad QRS)

records.label: Paced rhythm

rois.R: Rate about 55, not quite regular. The gaps vary between beats.
rois.O: Every QRS is broad with a deep negative complex in V1–V4. Pacing spikes are not clearly visible on this recording, so the broad, uniform QRS is the main clue to pacing. Small deflections before each QRS in II may be atrial activity that the pacemaker is following, which could explain the varying rate.
rois.I: QRS broad, a left bundle branch block-like shape typical of right ventricular pacing.
rois.S: ST and T point opposite to the main QRS, as expected with pacing. Baseline drift at the start of the limb leads and V6.

findings: Paced rhythm (broad QRS; spikes not clearly visible)

rois.R: Rate about 74, regular sinus rhythm, interrupted by one early beat near the end. (The auto-measured rate of 37 is wrong. Count it yourself.)
rois.O: A P wave before each normal QRS. The beat at about 8.3 s is early, broad and bizarre with no P wave before it, followed by a pause. That is a ventricular ectopic.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow on the sinus beats.
rois.S: No ST shift on the sinus beats. The ectopic has its own abnormal ST/T, which is expected.

rois.R: Rate about 78, sinus, with one early beat. The gaps also vary a little with breathing.
rois.O: A P wave before each normal QRS. The beat at about 7.9 s is early, broad and bizarre with no P wave, and it is followed by a long pause before the next sinus beat. That is a ventricular ectopic with a compensatory pause.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow on the sinus beats.
rois.S: No ST shift on the sinus beats.

records.label: Atrial ectopics

rois.R: Rate about 80, mostly regular, with a few beats arriving early.
rois.O: Most beats are sinus. Some early beats are narrow and the same shape as normal: atrial ectopics. The early beat at about 8.3 s is different. It is broad and abnormally shaped, so compare it closely with the narrow early beats and ask whether it is ventricular, or an atrial beat conducted aberrantly.
rois.I: PR normal, QRS narrow on the sinus beats.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift on the sinus beats. Baseline drift in V1.

findings: One broad early beat (ventricular or aberrant)

rois.R: Irregular. A sinus rhythm broken up by early beats, some arriving in quick succession. Overall rate about 85.
rois.O: The early beats are narrow and look like the normal beats, so they come from above the ventricles (atrial ectopics). An early atrial beat may carry a differently shaped P wave, often hidden in the preceding T wave, so look at the T wave before each early beat.
rois.I: QRS narrow. Note the notched QRS in V1.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift. Baseline wander in the limb leads at the start of the strip.

records.label: Complete heart block

rois.R: Slow and regular ventricular rate, about 37.
rois.O: P waves are present, best seen in V1, at about 80 a minute. They march through at their own steady rate, some landing just before a QRS, some just after, some in the gap. The P waves and QRS complexes are not linked.
rois.I: No consistent PR interval. It changes beat to beat because the atria and ventricles are working independently. That is complete heart block. The QRS is at the broad end with an RSR' shape in V1.
rois.S: No convincing ST shift.

findings: Atrial rate about 80, ventricular rate about 37
P waves and QRS complexes dissociated

rois.R: No rate can be counted and no rhythm can be found. The trace is chaotic and irregular throughout.
rois.O: No P waves and no identifiable QRS complexes. Just disorganised waves of varying shape and size.
rois.I: No measurable PR, QRS or QT.
rois.S: No ST segment or T waves can be identified. Coarse ventricular fibrillation, present in all 12 leads.

rois.R: No true rate or rhythm. Fast, chaotic waves that rise and fall in size across the strip.
rois.O: No P waves and no proper QRS complexes. In places, particularly V2–V4, the waves look fairly regular for a second or two. Don't be fooled. Look across all the leads and the whole strip: the shape and size keep changing.
rois.I: No measurable intervals.
rois.S: No ST segment or T waves. Ventricular fibrillation.

records.label: Ventricular fibrillation

rois.R: No rate or rhythm. Irregular, disorganised waves.
rois.O: No P waves and no identifiable QRS complexes. The waves are smaller in the limb leads than in the chest leads, so finer VF can look almost flat in some leads. Always check more than one lead before calling asystole.
rois.I: No measurable intervals.
rois.S: No ST segment or T waves. Note V6 has a large baseline shift at the start, which is lead artefact, not part of the rhythm.

findings: Ventricular fibrillation (finer in the limb leads)

rois.R: Fast and regular, about 165. Broad-complex tachycardia.
rois.O: No P waves can be seen. Every complex is broad and identical (monomorphic): positive in II, III and aVF, and negative in V1–V2.
rois.I: QRS broad, well over three small squares. A regular broad-complex tachycardia should be considered VT until proven otherwise. That is the finding.
rois.S: ST and T cannot be assessed independently in VT. They are distorted by the abnormal QRS. Ignore the last fraction of a second, where the trace flattens.

rois.R: Very fast and regular, about 195. Broad-complex tachycardia.
rois.O: No P waves can be seen. Every complex is broad and the same shape: deep negative in V1–V2 and aVR, upright in V4–V6.
rois.I: QRS broad. At this rate there is almost no flat baseline between complexes, and the QRS and T merge into one continuous wave.
rois.S: ST and T cannot be assessed independently. They are part of the abnormal ventricular complex.

rois.R: Regular, about 125. VT doesn't have to be very fast; this is a slower one.
rois.O: No P waves can be seen. The complexes are very broad and the same overall shape: upright in V1 and negative in V4–V6, the reverse of normal chest-lead progression.
rois.I: QRS very broad. A few complexes in the middle of the strip vary slightly in shape, so look closely, but the overall pattern stays broad and regular.
rois.S: ST and T cannot be assessed independently in VT. They are distorted by the abnormal QRS.
